query_text: Write the history of a colour.

content.text:
## A Short History of Purple

Purple has never been just a colour. For much of human history, it was a signal: of wealth, holiness, danger, mystery, and power.

Its story begins not with paint, but with **shellfish**.

In the ancient Mediterranean, especially among the Phoenicians, a deep purple dye was made from sea snails of the *Murex* family. The process was difficult, smelly, and extraordinarily expensive. Thousands of snails were needed to produce a small amount of dye. The result was **Tyrian purple**, a rich, reddish-purple colour that did not fade easily in sunlight.

Because it was so costly, purple became associated with rulers. In Rome, purple clothing was restricted by status. Senators wore garments edged with purple; emperors wore more of it. To be “born in the purple” meant to be born into imperial privilege. Colour became law, and law became theatre: purple showed who stood above whom.

Purple also entered religion. In Christianity, it came to signify **penitence, solemnity, and spiritual authority**. It is still used in the liturgical seasons of Advent and Lent. This double meaning—royal splendour and sacred seriousness—gave purple a strange emotional range. It could suggest both majesty and mourning, luxury and humility.

For centuries, purple remained rare. Artists used mineral pigments and plant dyes to approximate it, but a true, vivid, affordable purple was difficult to obtain. Then, in 1856, everything changed.

An 18-year-old English chemist named **William Henry Perkin** was trying to synthesize quinine, a treatment for malaria. Instead, he accidentally produced a vivid purple substance from coal tar. He called it **mauveine**. This was one of the first synthetic dyes, and it transformed fashion, chemistry, and industry.

Suddenly, purple was no longer reserved for emperors, bishops, or the very rich. It could be worn by ordinary people. Mauve became wildly fashionable in the 1860s. Queen Victoria wore it; so did Empress Eugénie of France. What had once required crushed sea snails could now be manufactured in a laboratory.

This shift changed the meaning of purple. It kept its old associations with royalty and spirituality, but it also became modern, artificial, fashionable, even democratic. It belonged not only to palaces and churches, but to department stores, wallpapers, dresses, and advertisements.

In the 20th century, purple acquired new political and cultural meanings. It became associated with **women’s suffrage**, often paired with white and green. Later, it became linked to counterculture, psychedelia, and pop music—think of “Purple Haze” or Prince’s carefully cultivated world of purple glamour and sensuality.

Today, purple remains unstable in the best way. It is neither warm nor cool, neither red nor blue, but a tension between them. It can feel regal, mournful, magical, artificial, queer, spiritual, childish, luxurious, or rebellious depending on its shade and setting.

Perhaps that is why purple has lasted so powerfully in the imagination. It began as a colour wrested from the sea, became the property of emperors, passed through churches and laboratories, and ended up everywhere—from flags and flowers to pop icons and phone screens.

Purple’s history is the history of rarity becoming accessible, of power becoming style, and of a colour that has always seemed to mean more than it says.
